blocks.text: When a particle undergoes rectilinear motion, its displacement, velocity, and acceleration can have only one of two possible directions, along the line of motion.
In such cases, we do not use arrows or other vector symbols to represent direction; instead, we use positive and negative signs to indicate it:

items: One direction along the line is taken as positive.
The opposite direction is taken as negative.

blocks.text: This simplifies the representation of displacement, velocity, and acceleration in rectilinear motion.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Think of the number line. A particle on it can only go right or left, so a sign is enough to show the direction. Which way you call positive is your choice (east, upwards, towards the school...), but once chosen it must be kept for the whole question.
Average Velocity
The average velocity (\(v\)) of an object is defined as the total displacement divided by the total time taken:

blocks.latex: v_{avg} = \text{Average velocity} = \dfrac{\text{Total displacement}}{\text{Total Time}} = \dfrac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}
blocks.text_alt: v average equals average velocity equals total displacement over total time equals delta x over delta t

blocks.text: Average Speed
The average speed of an object is defined as the total distance travelled divided by the total time taken:

blocks.text_alt: average speed equals total distance travelled over total time

blocks.title: Recall!
blocks.text:
a body goes and come back starting position
Displacement = 0
Distance 0

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The Recall! box prints "a body goes and come back starting position" and then "Distance 0" with the relation sign missing between the two. It should read: when a body goes and comes back to its starting position, Displacement \(= 0\) but Distance \(\ne 0\) (the distance is the length of the whole path, which is not zero).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
\(\Delta x\) (read "delta x") means "change in \(x\)" = final position \(-\) initial position, and \(\Delta t\) = final time \(-\) initial time.
Average velocity uses displacement, so it can be negative or zero. Average speed uses distance, so it is never negative. When the particle never turns back, both have the same size; when it turns back, the average speed is larger.

blocks.title: Numbering note (ours)
blocks.text: The textbook prints no Example 1, and it prints the number "Example 2" twice on these two pages: first for the man walking east and then west, then for the particle with \(x(t) = t^{3} - 6t^{2}\). We show the first one as Example 1 and the second as Example 2. From Example 3 onwards the printed numbers are kept, so every later example can be found in the book under its own number.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.problem: A man walks 100 meters east in 2 minutes, then turns around and walks 60 meters west in 1 minute. Find his speed and velocity.
steps:
Given: 100 m east in 2 min, then 60 m west in 1 min.
To find: his average speed and his average velocity for the whole walk.
Method: average speed = total distance / total time (direction ignored); average velocity = total displacement / total time (direction kept with signs). Both are "averages" because we only know the totals, not his speed at each instant.

Step 1: Total distance and total time
\[\text{Total distance} = 100 + 60\]
\[= 160\ \text{meters}\]
\[\text{Total time} = 2 + 1 = 3\ \text{minutes}\]
Why: distance is a scalar, so the two pieces of the path are simply added, whatever their directions.

Step 2: Average speed
\[\text{Average speed} = \dfrac{\text{Total distance travelled}}{\text{Total Time}}\]
\[= \dfrac{160}{3}\]
\[= 53.3\ \text{meters/min}\]
Why: this is the definition of average speed; \(\frac{160}{3} = 53.33...\), written to one decimal place.

Step 3: Displacements with signs
Taking east as positive and west as negative:
\[x_{1} = 100\ \text{meters}\]
\[x_{2} = -60\ \text{meters}\]
\[\text{Total displacement} = x_{1} + x_{2}\]
\[= 100 - 60 = 40\ \text{meters}\]
Why: displacement is a vector; on a straight line its direction is shown by its sign, so the westward walk cancels part of the eastward walk. He ends 40 m east of his starting point.

Step 4: Average velocity
\[v_{avg} = \dfrac{\text{Total displacement}}{\text{Total Time}}\]
\[= \dfrac{40}{3}\]
\[= 13.33\ \text{meters/min (eastward)}\]
Why: definition of average velocity. The answer is positive, so its direction is the positive direction, east.

Check:
The magnitude of the average velocity can never be more than the average speed, because \(|\text{displacement}| \le \text{distance}\). Here \(13.33 \le 53.3\). They differ because he turned back; had he walked only east, the two would be equal.
blocks.answer: Average speed \(= \frac{160}{3} \approx 53.3\) meters/min; average velocity \(= \frac{40}{3} \approx 13.33\) meters/min towards the east.

blocks.text: Instantaneous Velocity

The instantaneous velocity is the rate of change of displacement with respect to time at a given instant. If \(x(t)\) is the displacement of a particle at any time \(t\), then instantaneous velocity \(v(t)\) at any time \(t\) is given by:

blocks.text_alt: v of t equals d x by d t

blocks.text: Instantaneous Speed
Instantaneous speed is the magnitude of instantaneous velocity:

blocks.text_alt: instantaneous speed equals modulus of v of t equals modulus of d x by d t

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why a derivative? Average velocity is \(\frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}\) over an interval. Make the interval shorter and shorter around one instant; the limit of \(\frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}\) as \(\Delta t \to 0\) is exactly the derivative \(\frac{dx}{dt}\). So instantaneous velocity is "average velocity over a very tiny time". A car's speedometer shows instantaneous speed.
The sign of \(v(t)\) gives the direction: \(v > 0\) moving in the positive direction, \(v < 0\) in the negative direction, \(v = 0\) momentarily at rest (this is where a particle can turn back).

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.problem: Let \(x(t) = t^{3} - 6t^{2}\) be the position of a particle moving along a straight line at any time \(t\), where \(x\) is in meters and \(t\) is in seconds. Find the velocity and the speed of the particle at any time \(t\) and at \(t = 1\) second.
steps:
Given: position \(x(t) = t^{3} - 6t^{2}\) (meters, seconds).
To find: velocity and speed at any time \(t\), and at \(t = 1\) s.
Method: instantaneous velocity is the derivative of position, \(v(t) = \frac{dx}{dt}\); instantaneous speed is its absolute value \(|v(t)|\).

Step 1: Differentiate with respect to \(t\)
\[\dfrac{dx}{dt} = 3t^{2} - 12t\]
Why: power rule, \(\frac{d}{dt}(t^{n}) = nt^{n-1}\): \(\frac{d}{dt}(t^{3}) = 3t^{2}\) and \(\frac{d}{dt}(6t^{2}) = 12t\).

Step 2: Velocity and speed at any time \(t\)
\[v(t) = 3t^{2} - 12t \quad \text{...(1)}\]
\[\text{Speed} = |v(t)| = |3t^{2} - 12t| \quad \text{...(2)}\]
Why: velocity is \(\frac{dx}{dt}\); speed is the magnitude of velocity, so we take the absolute value.

Step 3: Substitute \(t = 1\) into (1) and (2)
\[v(1) = 3(1)^{2} - 12(1)\]
\[= 3 - 12 = -9\ \text{meter/second}\]
\[\text{Speed} = |v(1)| = |-9| = 9\ \text{m/s}\]
Why: put \(t = 1\) in the formulas of Step 2. The minus sign means that at \(t = 1\) s the particle is moving in the negative direction; the speed has no sign.

Check:
At \(t = 1\), \(x = 1 - 6 = -5\) m; at \(t = 1.01\), \(x = 1.030301 - 6.1206 = -5.090299\) m. In 0.01 s the position changed by about \(-0.09\) m, that is about \(-9\) m/s, as found.

blocks.text: Acceleration
Rate of change of velocity with respect to time is called acceleration. If \(v(t)\) is velocity of a particle at any time \(t\), then its acceleration \(a(t)\) is given by:

blocks.text_alt: a of t equals d v by d t

blocks.text: Since \(v = \frac{dx}{dt}\), the above expression can also be written as:

blocks.text_alt: a of t equals d v by d t equals d by d t of d x by d t equals second derivative of x with respect to t

blocks.text: If velocity \(v\) of the particle is given as a function of displacement \(x\): Using the Chain Rule:

blocks.text_alt: a equals d v of x by d t equals d v by d x times d x by d t

blocks.text: But since \(v = \frac{dx}{dt}\), we get:

blocks.text_alt: a equals v times d v by d x

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Which formula when?
1. \(v\) given as a function of \(t\): use \(a = \frac{dv}{dt}\).
2. \(x\) given as a function of \(t\): differentiate twice, \(a = \frac{d^{2}x}{dt^{2}}\).
3. \(v\) given as a function of \(x\) (no \(t\) in sight): use \(a = v\frac{dv}{dx}\). The chain rule lets us go "through \(x\)" because \(v\) depends on \(x\) and \(x\) depends on \(t\).
For instance, in Example 2, \(a(t) = \frac{d}{dt}(3t^{2} - 12t) = 6t - 12\), so \(a(1) = -6\) m/s\(^{2}\). At \(t = 1\) both \(v\) and \(a\) are negative (same sign), so the particle is speeding up in the negative direction. When \(v\) and \(a\) have opposite signs the particle is slowing down.
Units of Acceleration
If displacement is measured in meters and time is in seconds, then unit of acceleration is meters per second square i.e. m/s\(^{2}\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Why "per second squared"? Acceleration is change of velocity (m/s) per second: \(\frac{\text{m/s}}{\text{s}} = \text{m/s}^{2}\). An acceleration of \(2\) m/s\(^{2}\) means the velocity grows by \(2\) m/s every second.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. On a straight line, direction is shown by the sign: one direction positive, the other negative.
2. Average velocity \(= \frac{\text{total displacement}}{\text{total time}} = \frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}\); average speed \(= \frac{\text{total distance}}{\text{total time}}\).
3. Instantaneous velocity \(v = \frac{dx}{dt}\); instantaneous speed \(= |v|\).
4. Acceleration \(a = \frac{dv}{dt} = \frac{d^{2}x}{dt^{2}} = v\frac{dv}{dx}\); unit m/s\(^{2}\).
5. \(v\) and \(a\) with the same sign: speeding up; opposite signs: slowing down.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Using total distance in average velocity (or displacement in average speed). Read which one is asked.
2. Taking average speed as the average of two speeds. In Example 1 the speeds are 50 and 60 m/min, but the average speed is \(\frac{160}{3} \approx 53.3\), not 55: always divide the total distance by the total time.
3. Writing a negative speed: speed is \(|v|\), never negative.
4. Using \(a = \frac{dv}{dt}\) when \(v\) is given in terms of \(x\); there use \(a = v\frac{dv}{dx}\).
